<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:intro-higher}
For every $m\ge3$ there is a connected cosimple matroid $M$ of rank $m$ and corank three with nonzero classes $\alpha_i\in T^1_{-\mathbf e_i}(M)$, $0\le i<m$, over every field, such that:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}]
\item every proper subcollection admits a joint deformation over its polynomial parameter ring;
\item all the classes admit a flat joint deformation over $k[t_0,\ldots,t_{m-1}]/(t_0\cdots t_{m-1})$;
\item the resulting deformation modulo $(t_0,\ldots,t_{m-1})^m$ cannot lift modulo $(t_0,\ldots,t_{m-1})^{m+1}$, even in the ungraded category.
\end{enumerate}
Within the fine-multigraded category, with $\deg t_i=\mathbf e_i$, the jet in \textup{(3)} is uniquely determined by its first-order classes. Its first essential obstruction has order $m$, although all pairwise primary cup products vanish.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:intro-graph}
Write a fine degree uniquely as $\mathbf c=\mathbf a-\mathbf b$, where $\mathbf a,\mathbf b\in\mathbb N^{E(M)}$ have disjoint supports.  A component $T^2_{\mathbf c}(M)$ vanishes unless $\mathbf b=\mathbf 1_B$ is nonzero and squarefree, $A=\operatorname{supp}\mathbf a$ is independent, and $B$ consists of actual vertices of $L=\operatorname{lk}_M A$.  Under these conditions, set $N=L^*$.  Then, over every field,
\[
T^2_{\mathbf c}(M)
\cong
\bigoplus_{\substack{H\text{ hyperplane of }N\\H\cap B=\varnothing}}
\widetilde H^0(\Gamma_B(H);k).
\]
The analogous formula for $T^1$, which recovers in dual form the description of Brehm and Constantinescu \cite{BrehmConstantinescu}, is given in Theorem~\ref{thm:universal-graph}.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:intro-vanishing}
For a finite matroid $M$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}]
\item $T^2(M)=0$;
\item $T^2_{-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(M)=0$ for all distinct $p,q\in E(M)$;
\item every connected component of $M$ has corank at most two;
\item every cocircuit of $M$ has size at most three;
\item $M$ has no minor isomorphic to $U_{1,4}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:intro-cup}
For every matroid $M$, every pair of distinct actual vertices $p,q$, and every field $k$, the cup product
\[
T^1_{-\mathbf e_p}(M)\otimes_k T^1_{-\mathbf e_q}(M)
\longrightarrow T^2_{-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(M)
\]
is surjective.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:intro-all-rank}
Let $M$ be connected with $\operatorname{rk} M\ge2$ and $\operatorname{corank} M\ge3$.  There are distinct $e,p,q\in E(M)$ for which
\[
T^1_{\mathbf e_e-\mathbf e_p}(M)\otimes_kT^1_{\mathbf e_e-\mathbf e_q}(M)
\twoheadrightarrow
T^2_{2\mathbf e_e-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(M)\ne0.
\]
All three fine degrees have standard total degree zero.  Over every field, some standard-degree-zero first-order deformation fails to lift from $k[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$ to $k[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^3)$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:intro-dichotomy}
For every field $k$ and every matroid $M$, the affine deformation functor of $k[M]$ is formally smooth if and only if every connected component of $M$ has corank at most two, if and only if $M$ has no $U_{1,4}$-minor.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:localization}
Let $R$ be a finitely presented $k$-algebra and $U\subset R$ a multiplicative set.  For $i=1,2$, flat localization gives natural isomorphisms
\[
U^{-1}T^i(R/k;R)\cong T^i(U^{-1}R/k;U^{-1}R),
\]
compatible with cup products.  For a vertex $v$ of a simplicial complex $\Delta$,
\[
k[\Delta]_{x_v}\cong k[\operatorname{lk}_\Delta v][x_v^{\pm1}]
\]
after deleting ghost vertices, and the corresponding positive cotangent cohomology is the Laurent extension of that of the link. If a fine degree $\mathbf a-\mathbf 1_B$ satisfies the support criterion and $v\in\operatorname{supp}\mathbf a$, localization followed by setting $x_v=1$ identifies this component with the component of the link obtained by deleting its $v$-coordinate. Iteration over $\operatorname{supp}\mathbf a$ gives \eqref{eq:link-formula}.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Choose a finite-free model for the cotangent complex through the degrees needed for $T^1$ and $T^2$.  Flat localization commutes with its dual and with cohomology.  The cup product is induced by composition of cochain-level lifts, so it also commutes with localization.

Inverting $x_v$ kills variables which are not vertices of the link and turns the remaining monomial relations into those of $\operatorname{lk}_\Delta v$. The transitivity triangle for the Laurent extension splits into the base-changed cotangent complex of the link and the free summand generated by $dx_v$. The free summand has no positive cotangent cohomology. If $v\in\operatorname{supp}\mathbf a$, increasing its positive exponent does not change the relative complex in \eqref{eq:AC-relative}; multiplication by $x_v$ is the identity under these identifications. Thus the localization direct limit is already represented by the original fine component. Removing the Laurent monomial by setting $x_v=1$ deletes that coordinate. The positive-support hypothesis is essential: localization need not preserve a component with zero $v$-coordinate.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:zero-dimensional}
Let $Z_D$ be the zero-dimensional complex on $d=|D|$ vertices.  For a nonzero squarefree $\mathbf b$,
\[
\dim_kT^2_{-\mathbf b}(Z_D)=
\begin{cases}
(d-3)_+,&\operatorname{supp}\mathbf b=\{p,q\},\ p\ne q,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
All components with nonempty positive support vanish.  Thus $T^2(Z_D)=0$ if and only if $d\le3$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
For $B=\{p,q\}$, the support is a minimal nonface and $\widetilde N_B$ is the discrete set indexed by $D\setminus\{p,q\}$.  The relevant group is its reduced zeroth cohomology, of dimension $(d-3)_+$.  Singleton support has vanishing first cohomology.  A support of size at least three is a nonminimal nonface, so the relative pair agrees and contributes zero.  A nonempty positive support has a simplex as its link.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:universal-graph}
Let $M$ be a matroid, write $\mathbf c=\mathbf a-\mathbf b$ with disjoint nonnegative parts, and put $A=\operatorname{supp}\mathbf a$.  If $\mathbf b=0$, if $\mathbf b$ is not squarefree, or if $A\notin M$, then $T^i_{\mathbf c}(M)=0$ for $i=1,2$.  Suppose $\mathbf b=\mathbf 1_B$ is nonzero, set $L=\operatorname{lk}_MA$, and assume that $B$ lies in the actual vertex set of $L$.  Put $N=L^*$.

If $|B|\ge2$, then
\begin{align}
T^1_{\mathbf c}(M)
&\cong
\bigoplus_{\substack{H\text{ hyperplane of }N\\
H\cap B=\varnothing\\\mathcal G_B(H)=\varnothing}}k,
\label{eq:universal-T1}\\
T^2_{\mathbf c}(M)
&\cong
\bigoplus_{\substack{H\text{ hyperplane of }N\\H\cap B=\varnothing}}
\widetilde H^0(\Gamma_B(H);k).
\label{eq:universal-T2}
\end{align}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:universal-dimension}
\dim_kT^2_{\mathbf c}(M)=
\sum_{\substack{H\text{ hyperplane of }N\\H\cap B=\varnothing}}
\bigl(\kappa(\Gamma_B(H))-1\bigr)_+.
\end{equation}
If $B=\{p\}$ and $\mathscr H_p(N)$ is the discrete set of hyperplanes avoiding $p$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:singleton-formula}
T^1_{\mathbf c}(M)\cong\widetilde H^0(\mathscr H_p(N);k),
\qquad T^2_{\mathbf c}(M)=0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The support criterion and \eqref{eq:link-formula} reduce the problem to $T^i_{-\mathbf 1_B}(N^*)$.  Assume first that $|B|\ge2$.  For $F\subseteq E\setminus B$, set
\[
X=E\setminus(F\cup B).
\]
Complementation and the dual-rank identity identify the Altmann--Christophersen pair, with its order reversed, with
\[
P_B=\{X\subseteq E\setminus B:\operatorname{rk}_NX<s,\ \operatorname{rk}_N(X\cup B)=s\}
\]
and
\[
Q_B=\{X\in P_B:\operatorname{rk}_N(X\cup\{b\})<s
\text{ for some }b\in B\}.
\]
Indeed, if $B'\subsetneq B$ and $D=B\setminus B'$, then
\[
E\setminus(F\cup B')=X\cup D.
\]
The condition $\operatorname{rk}_N(X\cup D)<s$ implies the singleton condition for every $b\in D$; conversely a singleton condition is obtained from $B'=B\setminus\{b\}$.  Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:PB-QB-relative}
T^i_{-\mathbf 1_B}(N^*)\cong
H^{i-1}(|P_B'|,|Q_B'|;k),\qquad i=1,2.
\end{equation}

Define
\[
c(X)=\operatorname{cl}_N(X)\setminus B.
\]
Because $X\subseteq c(X)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_NX$, the sets $X$ and $c(X)$ have the same closure.  Hence $c$ preserves every rank condition defining $P_B$ and $Q_B$; it is an ascending idempotent on $P_B$ and restricts to one on $Q_B$.  The closure-operator lemma \cite[Corollary~10.12, p.~1852]{Bjorner} gives homotopy equivalences on both spaces.  Applying the five lemma to the two long exact sequences of pairs yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:relative-closure}
H^\bullet(|P_B'|,|Q_B'|;k)
\cong H^\bullet(|c(P_B)'|,|c(Q_B)'|;k).
\end{equation}

If $X\in P_B\setminus Q_B$, then $\operatorname{rk}_N(X\cup\{b\})=s$ for every $b\in B$.  A single element raises rank by at most one, so $\operatorname{rk}_NX=s-1$, and no element of $B$ lies in $\operatorname{cl}_NX$.  Conversely, every hyperplane disjoint from $B$ has these properties.  Since $c$ preserves $Q_B$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:relative-hyperplanes}
c(P_B)\setminus c(Q_B)
=\{H:H\text{ is a hyperplane of }N,\ H\cap B=\varnothing\}.
\end{equation}

Fix such an $H$ and set
\[
\mathcal F_B(H)=
\{F\in\mathcal L(N):F\subsetneq H,\ \operatorname{rk}_N(F\cup B)=s\}.
\]
The elements of $c(P_B)$ strictly below $H$ are exactly the members of $\mathcal F_B(H)$.  Every relative chain contains a unique hyperplane from \eqref{eq:relative-hyperplanes}, and that hyperplane is its maximum.  Deleting it produces a chain in $c(Q_B)$, while deleting another vertex remains in the same block.  Thus the relative cochain complex splits, already at chain level, into the blocks
\[
\bigl(\operatorname{cone}\Delta\mathcal F_B(H),
\Delta\mathcal F_B(H)\bigr).
\]
It follows that
\begin{align}
T^1_{-\mathbf 1_B}(N^*)&\cong
\bigoplus_{H\cap B=\varnothing}
\widetilde H^{-1}(\Delta\mathcal F_B(H);k),
\label{eq:block-T1-flat}\\
T^2_{-\mathbf 1_B}(N^*)&\cong
\bigoplus_{H\cap B=\varnothing}
\widetilde H^0(\Delta\mathcal F_B(H);k).
\label{eq:block-T2-flat}
\end{align}

For $G\in\mathcal G_B(H)$, let
\[
\mathcal U_G=\Delta\{F\in\mathcal F_B(H):F\subseteq G\}.
\]
Each $\mathcal U_G$ is a cone with apex $G$.  These cones cover $\Delta\mathcal F_B(H)$: any qualifying flat extends within $H$ to a rank-$(s-2)$ flat, and the spanning condition is preserved under enlargement.  For $G_1,\ldots,G_m$, put $K=\bigcap_iG_i$.  The corresponding intersection is nonempty exactly when $\operatorname{rk}_N(K\cup B)=s$; in that case $K$ is its maximum.  Hence all nonempty finite intersections are contractible, and the finite nerve lemma \cite[Theorem~10.6(i), p.~1850]{Bjorner} applies.  The one-skeleton of the nerve is precisely $\Gamma_B(H)$.  Reduced $H^0$ depends only on this one-skeleton, so
\[
\widetilde H^0(\Delta\mathcal F_B(H);k)
\cong\widetilde H^0(\Gamma_B(H);k).
\]
Moreover $\mathcal F_B(H)$ is empty exactly when $\mathcal G_B(H)$ is empty.  Equations \eqref{eq:block-T1-flat} and \eqref{eq:block-T2-flat} now prove \eqref{eq:universal-T1}--\eqref{eq:universal-dimension}.  The low-rank cases are included by the empty-graph convention.

If $B=\{p\}$, adding $p$ raises rank by at most one, so every member of the complementary poset has rank $s-1$ and has closure avoiding $p$.  Closure retracts this poset to the antichain of hyperplanes avoiding $p$.  The reduced singleton form of the Altmann--Christophersen formula gives \eqref{eq:singleton-formula}.  Finally, \eqref{eq:link-formula} transports all formulas back to $M$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:T1-attribution}
For $T^1$, the formulas \eqref{eq:universal-T1} and \eqref{eq:singleton-formula} are, after dualization and \eqref{eq:link-formula}, a reformulation of the combinatorial description of the first cotangent cohomology of matroids obtained by Brehm and Constantinescu \cite{BrehmConstantinescu}.  We include the $T^1$ statements because the proof above yields both cohomological degrees simultaneously and because the singleton identification \eqref{eq:singleton-formula} supplies the coordinates for the cup products of Section~\ref{sec:cup}.  The graph $\Gamma_B(H)$ and the resulting $T^2$ statements are the contributions developed here.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:complete-Hilbert}
For $A\in M$ and $B\subseteq V(\operatorname{lk}_MA)$ with $|B|\ge2$, write $\Gamma^A_B(H)$ for the graph of \eqref{eq:graph-adjacency} associated with the dual matroid $(\operatorname{lk}_MA)^*$ and the set $B$, and define
\[
\omega_M(A,B)=
\sum_{\substack{H\text{ hyperplane of }(\operatorname{lk}_MA)^*\\H\cap B=\varnothing}}
\bigl(\kappa(\Gamma^A_B(H))-1\bigr)_+.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:complete-Hilbert}
\operatorname{Hilb}_{T^2(M)}(\mathbf t)=
\sum_{A\in M}
\left(\prod_{a\in A}\frac{t_a}{1-t_a}\right)
\left(
\sum_{\substack{B\subseteq V(\operatorname{lk}_MA)\\|B|\ge2}}
\omega_M(A,B)\prod_{b\in B}t_b^{-1}
\right).
\end{equation}
In particular, every multigraded dimension of $T^2(M)$ is independent of $\operatorname{char}k$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
The support criterion leaves precisely the displayed supports.  For fixed $A$, positive exponents contribute
\[
\prod_{a\in A}(t_a+t_a^2+\cdots)=
\prod_{a\in A}\frac{t_a}{1-t_a}.
\]
The graph formula supplies the coefficient of every squarefree negative support.  Singleton supports contribute nothing to $T^2$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:closure-strata}
For $M=N^*$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:closure-stratified}
\sum_{\substack{B\subseteq V(M)\\|B|\ge2}}
\dim_kT^2_{-\mathbf 1_B}(M)\prod_{b\in B}z_b
=
\sum_{K\in\mathcal L(N)}\sum_{H\text{ hyperplane}}
\omega_N(K,H)\Sigma_{K,H}(\mathbf z).
\end{equation}
If $I\subseteq B$ and $\operatorname{cl}_NI=\operatorname{cl}_NB$, then
\[
\dim_kT^2_{-\mathbf 1_B}(M)\le
\dim_kT^2_{-\mathbf 1_I}(M).
\]
If $B$ spans $N$, then $T^2_{-\mathbf 1_B}(M)=0$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Every graph rank condition depends on $B$ only through $\operatorname{cl}_NB$.  For fixed $K,H$, the supports contributing to the block are precisely the subsets of $K\setminus H$ which span $K$, proving \eqref{eq:closure-stratified}.  If $I\subseteq B$ has the same closure, the graphs agree and the hyperplanes avoiding $B$ form a subcollection of those avoiding $I$.  If $B$ spans, the bottom flat is a maximum-compatible cone point in every nonempty flat block, so each block is contractible.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:pair-block}
Let $M=N^*$ and let $p,q$ be distinct.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pair-block}
T^2_{-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(M)
\cong
\bigoplus_{\substack{H\text{ hyperplane of }N\\H\cap\{p,q\}=\varnothing}}
k^{\mathcal G_{\{p,q\}}(H)}/k\mathbf 1,
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pair-dim}
\dim_kT^2_{-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(M)=
\sum_{H\cap\{p,q\}=\varnothing}
(|\mathcal G_{\{p,q\}}(H)|-1)_+.
\end{equation}
If $\{p,q\}$ is dependent in $N$, this component vanishes.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Only the last assertion needs comment.  If $p,q$ are parallel nonloops, a rank-$(s-2)$ flat together with $\{p,q\}$ cannot span rank $s$, so all vertex sets are empty.  If one is a loop, no hyperplane avoids the pair.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:pure-cocircuit}
Let $D$ be a cocircuit of $M$, let $d=|D|\ge4$, and let $p,q\in D$ be distinct.  Then
\[
\dim_kT^2_{-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(M)\ge d-3.
\]
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
In $N=M^*$, the set $D$ is a circuit.  Put $I=D\setminus\{p,q\}$ and extend $I\cup\{p\}$ to a basis $I\cup\{p\}\cup Z$.  Let
\[
H=\operatorname{cl}_N(I\cup Z),\qquad
G_x=\operatorname{cl}_N((I\setminus\{x\})\cup Z),\quad x\in I.
\]
The fundamental circuit of $q$ with respect to this basis is $D$. Removing
$p$ from the basis gives the independent set $I\cup Z$ of rank $\operatorname{rk} N-1$;
neither $p$ nor $q$ belongs to its closure, the latter because its fundamental
circuit contains $p$. For $x\in I$, the set $(I\setminus\{x\})\cup Z$ has
rank $\operatorname{rk} N-2$, while adjoining $p,q$ gives a basis: this is fundamental
exchange at $x\in D$. Thus $G_x$ is a vertex of
$\Gamma_{\{p,q\}}(H)$. If $x\ne y$, then $x\in G_y$ but $x\notin G_x$,
so these vertices are distinct. There are $d-2$ of them, and
\eqref{eq:pair-dim} gives the bound.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:exact-cocircuit}
Let $D$ be a cocircuit of $M$, let $A$ be a basis of the complementary hyperplane, and put $d=|D|$.  For distinct $p,q\in D$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:exact-cocircuit}
\dim_kT^2_{\mathbf 1_A-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(M)=(d-3)_+.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
The link $\operatorname{lk}_MA$ is the zero-dimensional complex on $D$.  Apply \eqref{eq:link-formula} and Lemma~\ref{lem:zero-dimensional}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:bipartite}
Let $G$ be a connected bipartite graph with bipartition $L\sqcup R$, where $|L|\ge2$ and $|R|\ge3$.  There are distinct $x,y\in L$ such that
\[
N_G(x)\cap N_G(y)\ne\varnothing,
\qquad |N_G(x)\cup N_G(y)|\ge3.
\]
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Choose three vertices of $R$, a spanning tree of $G$, and the minimal subtree $T$ containing the chosen vertices.  Every leaf of $T$ is one of the chosen vertices and hence lies in $R$.

If some $z\in R\cap V(T)$ has degree at least two in $T$, choose distinct neighbors $x,y\in L$.  Neither is a leaf, so each has a further neighbor in $R$; the two further neighbors are distinct because $T$ has no cycle.  Otherwise every $R$-vertex of $T$ has degree one.  Bipartiteness then forces $T$ to be a star with center $x\in L$, adjacent to all three chosen vertices.  Since $|L|\ge2$ and $G$ is connected, a path from $x$ to another $L$-vertex begins $x,z,y$.  Thus $x,y$ have a common neighbor, while $x$ already has the three chosen neighbors.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:rank-two-reduction}
Let $M$ be connected of rank $r\ge2$ and corank at least three.  From any basis $B$ one can find distinct $x,y\in B$ such that, after contracting $A_0=B\setminus\{x,y\}$ and deleting loops, the resulting rank-two matroid has at least five elements and at least three parallel classes; in particular, it is connected.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:bipartite} to the connected fundamental graph $G_B(M)$, with sides $B$ and $E\setminus B$.  The chosen $x,y$ have a common nonbasis neighbor and at least three nonbasis neighbors in total.  After contracting $A_0$, all these neighbors remain nonloops, so together with $x,y$ there are at least five elements.  If $e$ is a common neighbor, then
\[
C_{M/A_0}(e;\{x,y\})=\{x,y,e\},
\]
so $x,y,e$ lie in three different parallel classes.  Finally, a loopless rank-two matroid with at least three parallel classes is connected: a disconnected one is a direct sum of two nonempty loopless matroids of rank one and has exactly two parallel classes.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:large-cocircuit}
Every connected matroid of corank at least three has a cocircuit of size at least four.  If $r=\operatorname{rk} M\ge2$, there is an independent $(r-1)$-set $A$ such that
\[
D=E(M)\setminus\operatorname{cl}_MA
\]
is such a cocircuit.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
A connected rank-zero matroid has at most one element, so the corank
hypothesis excludes that case. If $r=1$, connectedness gives $M=U_{1,n}$
with $n\ge4$, and $E$ itself is a cocircuit. Assume $r\ge2$ and use
Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-two-reduction}. Let $N$ be the loopless rank-two
contraction, let $m=|E(N)|\ge5$, and choose a smallest parallel class $P$.
Since there are at least three classes,
\[
|E(N)\setminus P|\ge m-\lfloor m/3\rfloor\ge4.
\]
Choose $v\in P$ and put $A=A_0\cup\{v\}$.  The loops created by contracting $A_0$ already lie in $\operatorname{cl}_MA_0$, while the other elements in $\operatorname{cl}_MA$ correspond exactly to $P$.  Thus
\[
E(M)\setminus\operatorname{cl}_MA=E(N)\setminus P.
\]
The closure of $A$ is a hyperplane, so this complement is the required cocircuit.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:vanishing}
For a finite matroid $M$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}]
\item $T^2(M)=0$;
\item $T^2_{-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(M)=0$ for all distinct $p,q\in E(M)$;
\item every connected component of $M$ has corank at most two;
\item $M$ is a direct sum of matroids of corank at most two;
\item every cocircuit of $M$ has size at most three;
\item $M$ has no $U_{1,4}$-minor.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The first condition implies the second.  If the second holds, Proposition~\ref{prop:pure-cocircuit} excludes cocircuits of size at least four, giving (5).  If (5) holds and some connected component had corank at least three, Theorem~\ref{thm:large-cocircuit} would give a contradiction.  Thus (3) holds, and (3) is equivalent to (4) by the component decomposition.  Condition (4) implies (1) by the known corank-two vanishing and \eqref{eq:direct-sum-T2}.  Also, (3) directly implies (5), since cocircuits lie in components and are circuits of duals of rank at most two.

If $D$ is a cocircuit and $H=E\setminus D$, then $M/H\cong U_{1,|D|}$.  A cocircuit of size at least four therefore produces a $U_{1,4}$-minor.  Conversely, deletion and contraction do not increase corank, and minors of a direct sum are direct sums of minors.  Hence a direct sum of corank-at-most-two components has no $U_{1,4}$-minor.  This proves the remaining equivalence.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:conjecture}
The vanishing conjecture in \cite[Conjecture~22]{CKNSV} holds.  The class of matroids with $T^2=0$ is minor-closed and has the unique excluded minor $U_{1,4}$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
No monotonicity assertion for the module $T^2$ under arbitrary minors is needed.  Only its vanishing class is being identified with a minor-closed matroid class.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:top-strand}
Let $\mathbf c=\mathbf a-\mathbf b$ have disjoint nonnegative parts, suppose $|\operatorname{supp}\mathbf a|=r-1$, and put $A=\operatorname{supp}\mathbf a$.  Then
\[
\dim_kT^2_{\mathbf c}(M)=
\begin{cases}
(d_A-3)_+,&A\in M,\ \mathbf b=\mathbf e_p+\mathbf e_q,
\ \{p,q\}\in\binom{D_A}{2},\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus every nonzero component in this strand has two-element squarefree negative support, and its dimension is independent of the positive exponents and of $k$.
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
For an independent $(r-1)$-set $A$, the link is $Z_{D_A}$.  Apply the support criterion, \eqref{eq:link-formula}, and Lemma~\ref{lem:zero-dimensional}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:finite-detector}
For every matroid $M$,
\[
T^2(M)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad W(M)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\Theta(M)=0.
\]
If $M$ is connected, $r\ge2$, and $\operatorname{corank} M\ge3$, neither $W(M)$ nor the full rank-one-link strand generates $T^2(M)$ as a $k[M]$-module.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Every cocircuit is complementary to a hyperplane, and every hyperplane has a basis $A$.  Theorem~\ref{thm:top-strand} and Theorem~\ref{thm:vanishing} prove the equivalences.  Under the hypotheses in the second assertion, Proposition~\ref{prop:pure-cocircuit} supplies a nonzero purely negative component.  Multiplication by a monomial only increases fine degree, so an element with nonempty positive support cannot generate it.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:top-series}
The fine Hilbert series of the rank-one-link strand is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:top-fine-series}
\sum_{\substack{A\in M\\|A|=r-1}}
(d_A-3)_+
\left(\sum_{\{p,q\}\in\binom{D_A}{2}}t_p^{-1}t_q^{-1}\right)
\prod_{a\in A}\frac{t_a}{1-t_a}.
\end{equation}
If $b(N)$ denotes the number of bases of $N$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Theta-cocircuit}
\Theta(M)=
\sum_{D\text{ cocircuit of }M}
b(M|(E\setminus D))\binom{|D|}{2}(|D|-3)_+.
\end{equation}
After setting every $t_e=t$ in \eqref{eq:top-fine-series}, the series becomes
\begin{equation}\label{eq:top-coarse-series}
\frac{t^{r-3}}{(1-t)^{r-1}}\Theta(M).
\end{equation}
In particular, for $j\ge0$ and $r\ge2$, the part of standard degree $r-3+j$ has dimension
\[
\Theta(M)\binom{r+j-2}{r-2}.
\]
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
The first formula follows by summing the positive exponents in Theorem~\ref{thm:top-strand}.  Grouping $(r-1)$-sets by their closures gives \eqref{eq:Theta-cocircuit}: the sets spanning $E\setminus D$ are its bases.  The specialization and coefficient extraction are immediate.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:Theta-profiles}
Let $N=M^*$.  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Theta-circuit}
\Theta(M)=\sum_{C\text{ circuit of }N}b(N/C)f(|C|).
\end{equation}
Equivalently, if $q_d(N)$ counts spanning subsets of size $\operatorname{rk} N+1$ whose unique circuit has size $d$, then
\[
\Theta(M)=\sum_d f(d)q_d(N).
\]
For a basis $B$ of $M$ and $e\in B$, let
\[
D^*(B;e)=E\setminus\operatorname{cl}_M(B\setminus\{e\}),
\qquad d_B(e)=|D^*(B;e)|.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Theta-basis-average}
\Theta(M)=\sum_{B\text{ basis of }M}\sum_{e\in B}h(d_B(e)).
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Duality gives $(M|(E\setminus D))^*=N/D$ for a cocircuit $D$, so \eqref{eq:Theta-cocircuit} becomes \eqref{eq:Theta-circuit}.  Extending a basis of $N/C$ by $C$ is a bijection to spanning nullity-one sets with unique circuit $C$.  For the basis average, map $(B,e)$ to $A=B\setminus\{e\}$.  A fixed $A$ has exactly $d_A$ preimages, and $d_Ah(d_A)=f(d_A)$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:uniform-bounds}
Let $M$ have rank $r\ge1$, $n$ elements, and corank $c=n-r\ge3$.  Then
\begin{align}
\Theta(M)&\le b(M)\,r\,\frac{c(c-2)}2,
\label{eq:uniform-bound-one}\\
\Theta(M)&\le
\binom n{r-1}\binom{c+1}{2}(c-2).
\label{eq:uniform-bound-two}
\end{align}
Equality in either bound holds if and only if $M=U_{r,n}$.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Every fundamental cocircuit has size at most $c+1$, and $h$ is increasing on the relevant range.  Formula \eqref{eq:Theta-basis-average} proves \eqref{eq:uniform-bound-one}.  Formula \eqref{eq:Theta-definition} proves \eqref{eq:uniform-bound-two}.  Equality forces every independent $(r-1)$-set to be closed.  If a circuit had size at most $r$, deleting one of its elements and extending the remainder to an $(r-1)$-set would contradict closedness.  Hence every set of size at most $r$ is independent, so $M=U_{r,n}$.  The converse is immediate.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{cor:Theta-direct-sum}
For matroids on disjoint ground sets,
\[
\Theta(M_1\oplus M_2)=
\Theta(M_1)b(M_2)+b(M_1)\Theta(M_2).
\]
Consequently $\Theta(M)/b(M)$ is additive over connected components.
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
An independent set one element short of a basis of a direct sum is a basis in one summand and one element short in the other.  Its complementary cocircuit lies in the latter.  Split \eqref{eq:Theta-definition} into the two cases.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:Tutte-contrast}
The Tutte polynomial of $M$ determines whether $T^2(M)$ vanishes.  It does not determine $\Theta(M)$ or the coarse rank-one-link Hilbert series.
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
The Tutte polynomial is multiplicative under direct sums, and the polynomial of a connected matroid is irreducible in $\mathbb Z[x,y]$ \cite{MerinoDeMierNoy}.  Unique factorization therefore recovers the polynomial of each connected component.  The $y$-degree is its corank, so Theorem~\ref{thm:vanishing} decides vanishing.

For the negative statement, let $G_1,G_2$ be the graphs on $\{0,\ldots,6\}$ with edge sets
\begin{align*}
E(G_1)&=\{04,06,14,15,16,23,25,26,34,35,36,45,56\},\\
E(G_2)&=\{01,02,03,05,12,14,15,23,25,26,34,45,56\}.
\end{align*}
Direct rank-subset expansion gives identical Tutte polynomials.  The numbers of spanning two-forests with $|E\setminus\operatorname{cl}(A)|=d$, for $d=2,\ldots,8$, are respectively
\[
(209,235,141,130,101,41,5)
\]
and
\[
(225,198,162,138,89,46,4).
\]
Weighting by $f(d)$ gives
\[
\Theta(M(G_1))=12135,
\qquad
\Theta(M(G_2))=12161.
\]
The computation is independently verified as described in Section~\ref{sec:verification}.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:reconstruction}
For each independent $(r-1)$-set $A$, form a labeled graph on $E\setminus A$ by making $\{p,q\}$ an edge exactly when
\[
\dim_kT^2_{\mathbf 1_A-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(M)>0.
\]
If $d_A\le3$, this graph is empty.  If $d_A\ge4$, its nonisolated vertex set is $D_A$, the induced graph on $D_A$ is complete, and every edge has label $d_A-3$.  Hence the family of labeled fine components reconstructs all cocircuits of size at least four, including their sizes.  A fixed cocircuit $D$ occurs $b(M|(E\setminus D))$ times.
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
This is an immediate restatement of Theorem~\ref{thm:top-strand}.  Every cocircuit is the complement of a hyperplane and every hyperplane has a basis.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:rank-two-formulas}
Let $L$ be a loopless rank-two matroid with parallel classes $P_1,\ldots,P_t$ of sizes $n_1,\ldots,n_t$, and put $n=\sum_i n_i$.  Every purely negative component vanishes except in the following cases.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}]
\item If $B=\{p,q\}\subset P_i$, then
\[
\dim_kT^2_{-\mathbf 1_B}(L)=
\left(n_i-3+
\sum_{\substack{a<c\\a,c\ne i}}n_an_c\right)_+.
\]
\item If $p\in P_i$, $q\in P_j$, and $i\ne j$, then
\[
\dim_kT^2_{-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(L)=
\sum_{k\ne i,j}n_k(n-3-n_k)_+.
\]
\item Suppose $B$ consists of three elements from three distinct parallel classes.  If all elements of $L\setminus B$ lie in at most one parallel class, then
\[
\dim_kT^2_{-\mathbf 1_B}(L)=(n-4)_+;
\]
otherwise the component is zero.
\end{enumerate}
Every singleton negative component of $T^2(L)$ vanishes.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
The circuits of $L$ are the pairs within a parallel class and the triples meeting three different classes.  A squarefree negative support which is a nonface but not a circuit has equal relative terms and contributes zero.

In (1), $B$ is a circuit. The order-complex incidence graph
$|\widetilde N_B(L)'|$ has one component for each of the $n_i-2$
remaining points of $P_i$, containing that point and all incident
edge-face vertices. Every edge joining two classes different from $P_i$
gives an isolated edge-face vertex. Reduced $H^0$ gives the formula.

In (2), $B$ is a basis.  Relative vertices are the points in $P_k$, $k\ne i,j$.  A point of $P_k$ is incident with $n-2-n_k$ edge-faces after deleting $p,q$, and its relative incidence block contributes $(n-3-n_k)_+$.  Summing over the $n_k$ points gives (2).

In (3), $B$ is a circuit and $|\widetilde N_B(L)'|$ is the barycentric subdivision of $L\setminus B$. It is connected if at least two parallel classes remain, and otherwise it is a discrete set of $n-3$ points. Finally, the singleton Altmann--Christophersen complex is an incidence graph whose two-face vertices have degree at most one. It is a forest, so its first cohomology vanishes.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{cor:next-to-top}
Let $M$ have rank $r\ge2$, let $\mathbf a\in\mathbb N^E$ have independent support $A$ of size $r-2$, and let $\mathbf b$ be nonzero, squarefree, and supported on actual vertices of $L=\operatorname{lk}_MA$.  Then
\[
T^2_{\mathbf a-\mathbf b}(M)\cong T^2_{-\mathbf b}(L),
\]
and Theorem~\ref{thm:rank-two-formulas} computes the right-hand side.  All remaining components with positive-support size $r-2$ vanish by the support criterion.
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- corollary-11: body_md -->
\label{cor:projective-plane}
Let $q\ge2$ be a prime power, let $M=PG(2,q)$, and put $\nu=q^2+q+1$,
\[
\alpha=q-3+\binom q2q^2,
\qquad
\gamma=q(q-1)(q^2-3).
\]
Then
\begin{align}
\dim_kT^2(M)_0
&=\Theta(M)+\nu\left((q+1)\binom q2\alpha
+\binom{q+1}{2}q^2\gamma\right)\label{eq:PG-first}\\
&=\frac{q(q-1)(q+1)(q^2+q+1)}4
\left(3q^5+2q^4-10q^3-3q^2+2q-6\right).
\label{eq:PG-polynomial}
\end{align}
In particular, $\dim_kT^2(F_7)_0=357$, with $126$ dimensions in the rank-one-link strand and $231$ in the rank-two-link strand.
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Every point link has $q+1$ parallel classes of size $q$.  The within-class and between-class pair contributions are exactly the first two cases of Theorem~\ref{thm:rank-two-formulas}; triple contributions vanish.  The support criterion shows that the rank-one and rank-two link contributions exhaust standard degree zero.  Formula \eqref{eq:PG-polynomial} is the expansion of \eqref{eq:PG-first} together with
\[
\Theta(PG(2,q))=(q^2+q+1)\binom{q+1}{2}\binom{q^2}{2}(q^2-3).
\]
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:cup-coordinate}
Represent source classes in \eqref{eq:T1-hyperplane-functions} by functions
\[
\phi:\mathscr H_p\to k,
\qquad
\psi:\mathscr H_q\to k,
\]
each modulo constants.  Under the block identification \eqref{eq:pair-block}, the $H$-block of their cup product is, up to the fixed orientation of that block,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:block-cup-coordinate}
\left[
\bigl(\phi(Q_G)-\phi(H)\bigr)
\bigl(\psi(P_G)-\psi(H)\bigr)
\right]_{G\in\mathcal G_{\{p,q\}}(H)}
\pmod{k\mathbf 1}.
\end{equation}
This formula is valid over every field.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
The Stanley--Reisner ideal has its monomial Taylor presentation over $\mathbb Z$.  The cup product on presentation cochains is obtained by lifting the images of monomial generators and substituting them into the binomial relation module.  This construction uses only addition, multiplication, and the coefficients $0,\pm1$, so its coordinate formula commutes with base change to any field.

For completeness, consider the relative edge indexed by $G\subset H$.  In the notation of Altmann and Christophersen, it is represented by
\[
f=E\setminus(H\cup\{p,q\})
\subset
g=E\setminus(G\cup\{p,q\}).
\]
Substitution in the presentation formula, taking $d=\varnothing$ for $f$ and $e=\{q\}$ for $g$, gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:raw-cup}
E_H(G)=
(\phi(H)-\phi(Q_G))\psi(P_G)+\psi(H)\phi(Q_G).
\end{equation}
The possible fourth term is zero because its argument does not lie in the singleton set.  Rearranging,
\[
E_H(G)=
-(\phi(Q_G)-\phi(H))(\psi(P_G)-\psi(H))
+\phi(H)\psi(H).
\]
The last term is constant in $G$ and vanishes in the quotient by $k\mathbf 1$; reversing the block orientation absorbs the remaining sign.  This is precisely \eqref{eq:block-cup-coordinate}.  The calculation is the specialization of \cite[Proposition~19]{AltmannChristophersen}, now observed at the integral monomial-presentation level.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{thm:pure-pair-surjectivity}
For every matroid $M$, every pair of distinct actual vertices $p,q$, and every field $k$, the cup product
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pure-pair-cup}
T^1_{-\mathbf e_p}(M)\otimes_kT^1_{-\mathbf e_q}(M)
\longrightarrow T^2_{-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(M)
\end{equation}
is surjective.
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Use $M=N^*$ and fix a target coordinate $(H_0,G_0)$ in \eqref{eq:pair-block}.  Put
\[
P_0=P_{G_0},\qquad Q_0=Q_{G_0},
\]
and
\[
\mathcal S(G_0)=
\{H:H\cap\{p,q\}=\varnothing,\ G_0\subset H\}.
\]
Define representatives of singleton classes by
\[
\phi(K)=
\begin{cases}
1,&K=Q_0,\\
1,&K\in\mathcal S(G_0)\setminus\{H_0\},\\
0,&\text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\qquad
\psi(K)=
\begin{cases}
1,&K=P_0,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
There is no conflict: $Q_0$ contains $q$, $P_0$ contains $p$, while every member of $\mathcal S(G_0)$ avoids both.

For any coordinate $(H,G)$, the second factor in \eqref{eq:block-cup-coordinate} can be nonzero only when $P_G=P_0$.  If also $G=G_0$, then $H\in\mathcal S(G_0)$ and the first factor is nonzero exactly for $H=H_0$.  If $P_G=P_0$ but $G\ne G_0$, then $Q_G\ne Q_0$ by \eqref{eq:three-intersections}.  Moreover $H\notin\mathcal S(G_0)$: otherwise
\[
G_0\subseteq H\cap P_0=G
\]
would force equality of the two rank-$(s-2)$ flats.  Hence the first factor is zero.  The resulting product is the coordinate delta vector at $(H_0,G_0)$, up to sign.  Such vectors span before passing to blockwise constants, so their images span the target.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- corollary-12: body_md -->
\label{cor:link-lifted-cup}
Let $A\in M$, and let $p,q$ be distinct actual vertices of $L=\operatorname{lk}_MA$.  Then
\[
T^1_{\mathbf 1_A-\mathbf e_p}(M)\otimes_k
T^1_{\mathbf 1_A-\mathbf e_q}(M)
\twoheadrightarrow
T^2_{2\mathbf 1_A-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(M).
\]
The target is identified with $T^2_{-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(L)$.
<!-- end corollary-12 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Iterate Lemma~\ref{lem:localization} over the variables indexed by $A$, use \eqref{eq:link-formula}, and transport Theorem~\ref{thm:pure-pair-surjectivity} across the resulting cup-compatible isomorphisms.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:one-contraction}
Let $M$ be connected with $\operatorname{rk} M\ge2$ and $\operatorname{corank} M\ge3$.  There is an element $e$ such that $M/e$, after deleting its loops, has a connected component of corank at least three.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
If $\operatorname{rk} M=2$, choose $e$ in a smallest parallel class $P$.  A connected rank-two matroid has at least three parallel classes, and $|E|\ge5$, so
\[
|E\setminus P|\ge |E|-\lfloor |E|/3\rfloor\ge4.
\]
After contracting $e$ and deleting $P\setminus\{e\}$, one obtains a connected rank-one matroid of corank at least three.

Suppose $\operatorname{rk} M\ge3$.  Proposition~\ref{prop:rank-two-reduction} gives an independent set $A_0$ of size $\operatorname{rk} M-2$ such that $M/A_0$, after deleting loops, is a connected rank-two matroid $R$ on at least five elements.  Choose $e\in A_0$ and let $L=M/e$ with its loops deleted.  Contracting $A_0\setminus\{e\}$ in $L$, and then deleting loops, produces $R$.  Contraction acts componentwise and cannot join components.  Contracting nonloops preserves corank, while deleting newly created loops can only decrease it.  Hence all nonloops of $R$ descend from a single connected component $C$ of $L$, with
\[
\operatorname{corank} C\ge\operatorname{corank} R\ge3.
\]
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{thm:degree-zero-cup}
Let $M$ be connected with $\operatorname{rk} M\ge2$ and $\operatorname{corank} M\ge3$.  There are distinct $e,p,q\in E(M)$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:degree-zero-surjection}
T^1_{\mathbf e_e-\mathbf e_p}(M)\otimes_k
T^1_{\mathbf e_e-\mathbf e_q}(M)
\twoheadrightarrow
T^2_{2\mathbf e_e-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(M)\ne0.
\end{equation}
Thus $T^1(M)_0\otimes_kT^1(M)_0\to T^2(M)_0$ has nonzero image over every field.
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Choose $e$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:one-contraction}, put $L=M/e$ after deleting loops, and let $C$ be a connected component of $L$ with corank at least three.  By Theorem~\ref{thm:large-cocircuit}, $C$ has a cocircuit $D$ of size at least four.  Choose distinct $p,q\in D$.  Proposition~\ref{prop:pure-cocircuit} gives
\[
T^2_{-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(C)\ne0.
\]
If $L=C\oplus C'$, the direct-sum formula, or equivalently the dual hyperplane blocks, embeds this component into the same fine component for $L$.  Theorem~\ref{thm:pure-pair-surjectivity} gives a surjection onto it.  Localization at $x_e$ and evaluation at $x_e=1$ give cup-compatible isomorphisms
\begin{align*}
T^1_{\mathbf e_e-\mathbf e_p}(M)&\cong T^1_{-\mathbf e_p}(L),\\
T^1_{\mathbf e_e-\mathbf e_q}(M)&\cong T^1_{-\mathbf e_q}(L),\\
T^2_{2\mathbf e_e-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(M)&\cong T^2_{-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(L).
\end{align*}
Transporting the surjection proves \eqref{eq:degree-zero-surjection}.  Each fine degree has total degree zero.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:graded-polarization}
Let $k$ be an arbitrary field and let $\operatorname{ob}:T^1(M)\to T^2(M)$ denote the primary obstruction map for lifting first-order deformations from $k[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$ to $k[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^3)$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}]
\item $\operatorname{ob}$ doubles the fine grading: for a fine-homogeneous class $\chi$ of degree $\mathbf c$, the class $\operatorname{ob}(\chi)$ lies in $T^2_{2\mathbf c}(M)$.  This component vanishes, so $\operatorname{ob}(\chi)=0$.
\item For all $\alpha,\beta\in T^1(M)$,
\[
\operatorname{ob}(\alpha+\beta)
=\operatorname{ob}(\alpha)+\operatorname{ob}(\beta)+\alpha\cup\beta.
\]
\end{enumerate}
In particular, for fine-homogeneous classes $\alpha,\beta$ of distinct fine degrees, $\operatorname{ob}(\alpha+\beta)=\alpha\cup\beta$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
Work with the monomial Taylor presentation of $I_M=(m_1,\ldots,m_r)$.  A first-order deformation with tangent class $\chi$ deforms the generators to $m_i+\epsilon g_i$, where $g_i\in S$ lifts $\chi(m_i)$.  For the pair relation of $(m_i,m_j)$ with least common multiple $u_{ij}$, first-order flatness provides an expression
\[
\frac{u_{ij}}{m_i}\,g_i-\frac{u_{ij}}{m_j}\,g_j
=\sum_k b^{ij}_k m_k
\qquad\text{in }S,
\]
with $b^{ij}_k$ chosen linearly in the tuple $(g_i)$.  A second-order lift $m_i+\epsilon g_i+\epsilon^2h_i$ exists if and only if the presentation cochain
\[
o(\chi):(i,j)\longmapsto
\Bigl[\,\sum_k b^{ij}_k\,g_k\Bigr]\in S/I_M
\]
is a coboundary; its class in $T^2(M)$ is the primary obstruction and is independent of all choices.  Every operation involved preserves the fine multigrading, and $o(\chi)$ is the composition of the linear map $\chi\mapsto b(\chi)$ with multiplication by the values of $\chi$.  Hence $o$ is a quadratic map, and for fine-homogeneous $\chi$ of degree $\mathbf c$ the cochain $o(\chi)$ is homogeneous of degree $2\mathbf c$.  By the support criterion, a nonzero fine component of $T^1$ has degree $\mathbf c=\mathbf a-\mathbf 1_B$ with $B\ne\varnothing$; the negative part of $2\mathbf c$ has an exponent $2$, so $T^2_{2\mathbf c}(M)=0$ and $\operatorname{ob}(\chi)=0$.  This proves (1).

Expanding $o(\alpha+\beta)$ bilinearly gives
\[
o(\alpha+\beta)=o(\alpha)+o(\beta)
+\Bigl[(i,j)\mapsto\sum_k\bigl(b^{ij}_k(\alpha)\,\beta(m_k)+b^{ij}_k(\beta)\,\alpha(m_k)\bigr)\Bigr].
\]
The mixed cochain is the substitution construction of Lemma~\ref{lem:cup-coordinate}, whose class is $\alpha\cup\beta$; the identity uses only the coefficients $0,\pm1$ of the monomial presentation and holds over every field.  This proves (2), and the final statement follows by combining (1) and (2).
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- corollary-13: body_md -->
\label{cor:actual-obstructions}
Let $k$ be an arbitrary field.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}]
\item If some connected component of $M$ has corank at least three, then some first-order affine deformation of $k[M]$ does not lift from $k[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$ to $k[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^3)$.
\item If $M$ is connected with $\operatorname{rk} M\ge2$ and $\operatorname{corank} M\ge3$, such a deformation can be chosen in standard degree zero.  Hence $\operatorname{Def}^{\mathrm{gr}}_M$ is not formally smooth, and any miniversal hull has a nonzero quadratic Kuranishi term.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-13 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
For (1), Theorem~\ref{thm:vanishing} provides a cocircuit of size at least four, and Proposition~\ref{prop:pure-cocircuit} then provides a nonzero purely negative pair target.  For (2), use the nonzero target in Theorem~\ref{thm:degree-zero-cup}.  In either case, surjectivity gives fine-homogeneous source classes $\alpha,\beta$ of distinct fine degrees with $\alpha\cup\beta\ne0$.  Lemma~\ref{lem:graded-polarization} gives
\[
\operatorname{ob}(\alpha+\beta)=\alpha\cup\beta\ne0,
\]
so the first-order deformation $\alpha+\beta$ does not lift to second order.  In (2), both source classes have standard degree zero.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- corollary-14: body_md -->
\label{cor:smoothness-dichotomy}
For every field $k$ and every matroid $M$, the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}]
\item $\operatorname{Def}_M$ is formally smooth;
\item $T^2(M)=0$;
\item every connected component of $M$ has corank at most two;
\item $M$ has no $U_{1,4}$-minor.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-14 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
(2)$\Rightarrow$(1) is standard, since all obstructions lie in $T^2(M)$.  (1)$\Rightarrow$(3) is the contrapositive of Corollary~\ref{cor:actual-obstructions}(1).  The equivalences (2)$\Leftrightarrow$(3)$\Leftrightarrow$(4) are part of Theorem~\ref{thm:vanishing}.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- corollary-15: body_md -->
\label{cor:graded-dichotomy}
Let $M$ be connected.  For every field $k$, the graded functor $\operatorname{Def}^{\mathrm{gr}}_M$ is formally smooth if and only if $\operatorname{rk} M\le1$ or $\operatorname{corank} M\le2$.
<!-- end corollary-15 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
If $\operatorname{corank} M\le2$, then $T^2(M)=0$.  If $\operatorname{rk} M\le1$, the only independent supports are the empty set and singletons; a singleton link of a rank-one matroid has empty actual vertex set, and singleton negative supports vanish by \eqref{eq:singleton-formula}, so every nonzero component of $T^2(M)$ is a purely negative block of negative standard total degree.  Hence $T^2(M)_0=0$ in both cases, and the graded functor, whose obstructions lie in $T^2(M)_0$, is formally smooth.  If $\operatorname{rk} M\ge2$ and $\operatorname{corank} M\ge3$, Corollary~\ref{cor:actual-obstructions}(2) shows that $\operatorname{Def}^{\mathrm{gr}}_M$ is not formally smooth.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:char-two}
In characteristic two the primary obstruction is a quadratic refinement of the cup product rather than one half of the cup square.  Lemma~\ref{lem:graded-polarization} shows that for matroid Stanley--Reisner rings this refinement carries no extra information: it vanishes on every fine-homogeneous class, so the whole quadratic map is determined by the bilinear cup product,
\[
\operatorname{ob}\Bigl(\sum_{\mathbf c}\chi_{\mathbf c}\Bigr)
=\sum_{\{\mathbf c,\mathbf c'\},\,\mathbf c\ne\mathbf c'}
\chi_{\mathbf c}\cup\chi_{\mathbf c'},
\]
the sum running over unordered pairs of distinct fine degrees.  In this sense the primary obstruction theory of this paper is characteristic-free.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{thm:arcs}
Let $k$ be an arbitrary field.  Represent classes by multigraded cocycles, so that $\chi\in T^1_{\mathbf c}(M)$ assigns to each circuit generator $m_i$ a multiple $\chi(m_i)\in S$ of the single monomial of multidegree $\deg m_i+\mathbf c$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}]
\item Suppose $\chi=\sum_j\chi_j$ with $\chi_j\in T^1_{\mathbf c_j}(M)$, and suppose that for every pair $(j,j')$, including $j=j'$, the vector $\mathbf c_j+\mathbf c_{j'}$ has an entry at most $-2$.  Then the $t$-linear family
\[
F_i=m_i+t\,\chi(m_i)
\]
is flat over $k[t]/(t^N)$ for every $N$: every Taylor relation lifts with coefficients linear in $t$, and no correction terms are needed.  This applies to every single fine-homogeneous class and, more generally, whenever the negative supports $B_j$ pairwise intersect and $\bigl(\bigcup_j\operatorname{supp}\mathbf a_j\bigr)\cap\bigl(\bigcup_jB_j\bigr)=\varnothing$.
\item Let $\alpha\in T^1_{\mathbf c_1}(M)$ and $\beta\in T^1_{\mathbf c_2}(M)$ with $\mathbf c_i=\mathbf a_i-\mathbf 1_{B_i}$, $B_1\cap B_2=\varnothing$, and $\operatorname{supp}(\mathbf a_1+\mathbf a_2)\cap(B_1\cup B_2)=\varnothing$.  Then $t(\alpha+\beta)$ lifts to $k[t]/(t^3)$ if and only if $\alpha\cup\beta=0$, and in that case a single multigraded correction $h$ of fine degree $\mathbf c_1+\mathbf c_2$ produces a family
\[
F_i=m_i+t\bigl(\alpha(m_i)+\beta(m_i)\bigr)+t^2h_i
\]
which is flat over $k[t]/(t^N)$ for every $N$.  Along these directions the cup product is the complete obstruction.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
A polynomial of fixed multidegree with a negative entry is zero. Least common multiples $u_{ij}$ of squarefree generators have exponents at most one, so every element of $S$ of multidegree $\deg u_{ij}+\mathbf d$ or $\deg m_i+\mathbf d$ vanishes identically whenever $\mathbf d$ has an entry at most $-2$.

We use the relation-lifting criterion for flatness over
$A_N=k[t]/(t^N)$. If generators $F_i$ lift the generators $m_i$ and every
generating relation among the $m_i$ lifts to a relation among the $F_i$,
then, for $J=(F_i)\subset A_N[x_e:e\in E]$, reduction identifies
$J/tJ$ with $I_M$. Tensoring the ideal sequence with $k$ therefore gives
$\operatorname{Tor}^{A_N}_1(A_N[x]/J,k)=0$. The local flatness criterion
for the nilpotent ideal $(t)$ gives $A_N$-flatness. The Taylor pair
relations generate the relation module of a monomial ideal, so it suffices
to lift those relations.

For (1), lift the Taylor relation of $(m_i,m_j)$ to first order as in Lemma~\ref{lem:graded-polarization}, with linear coefficient $-b^{ij}$.  The complete relation applied to $(F_i)$ has one remaining coefficient, at $t^2$, namely $-b^{ij}\cdot\chi(m_\bullet)$, a sum of terms of multidegrees $\deg u_{ij}+\mathbf c_\ell+\mathbf c_{\ell'}$, where $\ell,\ell'$ index the summands of $\chi$.  Each such term is identically zero by hypothesis, so the linear relation lift is an exact syzygy of $(F_i)$.  Lifting a generating set of relations proves flatness over every $k[t]/(t^N)$.  For the last assertion, an entry of $\mathbf c_\ell+\mathbf c_{\ell'}$ at an element of $B_\ell\cap B_{\ell'}$ equals $-2$ when $\ell\ne\ell'$, and at an element of $B_\ell$ equals $-2$ when $\ell=\ell'$, since the positive supports avoid all negative supports.

For (2), the second-order equation decomposes into fine degrees $2\mathbf c_1$, $\mathbf c_1+\mathbf c_2$, and $2\mathbf c_2$.  The doubled blocks vanish identically as in (1).  The mixed block is solvable exactly when the class $\alpha\cup\beta$ vanishes, by Lemma~\ref{lem:graded-polarization}; this proves the first assertion.  When $\alpha\cup\beta=0$, choose $h$ of fine degree $\mathbf c_1+\mathbf c_2$ solving the mixed block and lift each relation to second order.  Every higher coefficient of the lifted relation is a sum of terms whose fine degrees have the form $a\mathbf c_1+b\mathbf c_2$ with $a+b\ge3$.  Since $\max(a,b)\ge2$ and the positive supports avoid $B_1\cup B_2$, every such degree has an entry at most $-2$ on $B_1$ or $B_2$, so all these terms vanish identically and the quadratic relation lifts are exact syzygies of $(F_i)$.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- corollary-16: body_md -->
\label{cor:graphic}
For a finite graph $G$, $T^2(M(G))=0$ if and only if every cycle-matroid component has cyclomatic number at most two, equivalently every bond has size at most three. For a simple graph, this vanishing is equivalent to every edge-containing block being a bridge, a cycle, or a theta graph.

If $G$ is connected and deleting a bond $D$ gives components $G^D_1,G^D_2$, then
\[
\Theta(M(G))=
\sum_{D\text{ bond}}
\tau(G^D_1)\tau(G^D_2)
\binom{|D|}{2}(|D|-3)_+,
\]
where $\tau$ denotes the number of spanning trees and $\tau$ of a single vertex is one.
<!-- end corollary-16 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Cocircuits of $M(G)$ are bonds, and the corank of a cycle-matroid component is its cyclomatic number. The simple-block description follows from open-ear decomposition \cite[Proposition~3.1.1, pp.~59--60]{Diestel}: a cycle starts with cyclomatic number one, and each added ear increases it by one. A basis of $M(G)|(E\setminus D)$ is a spanning tree in each of the two components, so \eqref{eq:Theta-cocircuit} gives the formula.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- corollary-17: body_md -->
\label{cor:cographic}
For a finite graph $G$,
\[
T^2(M^*(G))=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{every cycle of $G$ has at most three edges}.
\]
For a simple graph, this vanishing is equivalent to every edge-containing block being a bridge or a triangle. If $G$ is connected, then
\[
\Theta(M^*(G))=
\sum_U f(\ell(U)),
\]
where $U$ ranges over connected spanning unicyclic subgraphs and $\ell(U)$ is the length of its unique cycle.
<!-- end corollary-17 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Cocircuits of $M^*(G)$ are graph cycles.  Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:vanishing}.  The simple-block statement again follows from open-ear decomposition.  The last formula is the nullity-one interpretation in Theorem~\ref{thm:Theta-profiles}.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:rank-two-closed-form}
For every connected rank-two matroid,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-two-closed-form}
\Theta(M)=\sum_i n_iF(n-n_i),
\qquad \dim_kT^2(M)_0=\Theta(M).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Every independent set of size $r-1$ is a single nonloop element $a$.  If $a\in P_i$, then $\operatorname{cl}_M(a)=P_i$ and the complementary cocircuit has size $n-n_i$.  The complementary hyperplane has $n_i$ bases, one for each element of $P_i$, so \eqref{eq:rank-two-extremal-cocircuit} gives the first formula.  For the standard total-degree-zero component, a positive support of size two has a rank-zero link and contributes nothing.  A positive support of size one must have exponent two; its rank-one link contributes only squarefree negative pairs.  Summing \eqref{eq:rank-two-extremal-Theta} over all singletons gives the second formula.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
\label{thm:rank-two-extremum}
Among connected rank-two matroids of corank $c\ge3$, the minimum of $\Theta$ is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-two-minimum}
\begin{cases}
6,&c=3,\\
32,&c=4,\\
81,&c=5,\\
168,&c=6,\\
c(c+1)(c-2),&c\ge7.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
Up to permutation of the classes, equality occurs for
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-two-equality-cases}
\begin{array}{c|c}
c&\text{parallel-class sizes}\\ \hline
3&(2,2,1)\\
4&(3,2,1)\\
5&(3,3,1)\\
6&(6,1,1)\text{ or }(4,3,1)\\
c\ge7&(c,1,1).
\end{array}
\end{equation}
For $c\ge7$ the equality class is unique.
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
Put $g_n(x)=xF(n-x)$.  By \eqref{eq:rank-two-closed-form}, we must minimize $\sum_i g_n(n_i)$ over partitions of $n=c+2$ into at least three positive parts.

First, let $u,v\ge1$ and $u+v\le n-2$, and write $w=n-u-v$.  If $w\ge4$, direct expansion gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-two-merge}
\begin{aligned}
2\bigl(g_n(u)+g_n(v)-g_n(u+v)\bigr)
={}&uv\bigl[u^2+v^2+3(u+v)w+6w^2\\
&\qquad-4(u+v)-16w+6\bigr]>0.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Indeed, $3w-4>0$ and $6w^2-16w+6>0$ for $w\ge4$.
If $w=2$ or $3$, then $g_n(u+v)=0$, while at least one of $g_n(u),g_n(v)$ is positive for $n\ge5$.  Thus every minimizer has exactly three parts.

Let $a\le b\le d$ and $a+b+d=n$.  If $a\ge2$, transfer one element from the smallest class to the largest and set
\[
\Delta=g_n(a)+g_n(d)-g_n(a-1)-g_n(d+1).
\]
With $A=a-2$, $U=b-a$, and $V=d-b$, expansion gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-two-transfer}
\begin{aligned}
2\Delta={}&8+24A+32U+12V+12A^2+45AU+27AV\\
&+34U^2+33UV+5V^2+12A^2U+12A^2V\\
&+21AU^2+24AUV+3AV^2+10U^3+15U^2V+6UV^2+V^3.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
All coefficients are positive, so a minimizing triple has the form $(1,b,d)$.

Finally let $s=b+d=n-1$ and $p=bd$.  For $b\ge2$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-two-final-comparison}
2\bigl(g_n(b)+g_n(d)-g_n(1)\bigr)=E(s,p),
\quad E(s,p)=-2p^2+(s^2-s-4)p-s(s-1)(s-3).
\end{equation}
For $n\ge9$, $E$ is concave on $2(s-2)\le p\le\lfloor s^2/4\rfloor$.  At the left endpoint,
\[
s^3-10s^2+25s-16>0,
\]
while at the right endpoint, writing $s=2m$ or $s=2m+1$ gives, respectively,
\[
2m(m^3-5m^2+6m-3)>0
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
2m^3(m-3)>0.
\]
Hence $b=1$ is the unique minimizer for $n\ge9$, with value
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-two-sparse-value}
2F(n-1)=(n-1)(n-2)(n-4)=c(c+1)(c-2).
\end{equation}
The cases $n=5,6,7,8$ are the four exceptional rows in \eqref{eq:rank-two-equality-cases}, obtained by direct enumeration of the three-part partitions.
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
\label{thm:integral-pair}
For every matroid $M$ and every pair of distinct actual vertices $p,q$, the
map \eqref{eq:integral-pair-map} for $N=M^*$ is a split surjection of
abelian groups.  Consequently its scalar extension is surjective over every
commutative ring.  Over a field $k$, the identifications
\eqref{eq:T1-hyperplane-functions} and \eqref{eq:pair-block} identify the
scalar extension with the cotangent cup product
\[
T^1_{-\mathbf e_p}(M)\otimes_kT^1_{-\mathbf e_q}(M)
\longrightarrow T^2_{-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(M).
\]
In particular,
\[
\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb Z}\mathsf L^2_{p,q}(M^*)
=\dim_kT^2_{-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(M),
\]
and every nonzero pair block remains a split cup-product quotient after
reduction modulo every prime.
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Fix a target coordinate $(H_0,G_0)$ and put
\[
P_0=\operatorname{cl}_{M^*}(G_0\cup\{p\}),\qquad
Q_0=\operatorname{cl}_{M^*}(G_0\cup\{q\}),
\]
\[
\mathcal S(G_0)=
\{H:H\text{ is a hyperplane of }M^*,\
H\cap\{p,q\}=\varnothing,\ G_0\subset H\}.
\]
Define integer-valued representatives by
\[
\phi(K)=
\begin{cases}
1,&K=Q_0,\\
1,&K\in\mathcal S(G_0)\setminus\{H_0\},\\
0,&\text{otherwise},
\end{cases}
\qquad
\psi(K)=
\begin{cases}
1,&K=P_0,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
There is no conflict because $Q_0$ contains $q$, $P_0$ contains $p$, and
every member of $\mathcal S(G_0)$ avoids both.  The proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:pure-pair-surjectivity}, now read over $\mathbb Z$, shows that
\eqref{eq:block-cup-coordinate} gives the coordinate delta class at
$(H_0,G_0)$, up to the fixed block orientation.  In each quotient
$\mathbb Z^{\mathcal G_{\{p,q\}}(H)}/\mathbb Z\mathbf 1$, all but one of the delta classes
form a basis.  Choosing their displayed decomposable preimages defines a
right inverse to \eqref{eq:integral-pair-map}.  Scalar extension preserves a
split epimorphism, and the fieldwise identification follows from the same
integer coordinate formula.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- corollary-18: body_md -->
\label{cor:unimodular-pair-cup}
After integral bases are chosen, every pure-pair cup matrix has Smith normal
form
\[
\operatorname{diag}(\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{
\operatorname{rank}\mathsf L^2_{p,q}},0,\ldots,0).
\]
Thus the pair obstruction quotient has an integral decomposable basis; its
dimension, nonvanishing pattern, and cup surjectivity are simultaneous over
all fields, including characteristic two.
<!-- end corollary-18 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
A split epimorphism between free abelian groups is integrally equivalent to a
projection onto a direct summand.  This is precisely the asserted Smith
normal form.
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:pure-pair-ranks}
For $p\ne q$ in $E(M)$, set
\[
V_p(M)=T^1_{-\mathbf e_p}(M),\qquad
W_{p,q}(M)=T^2_{-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(M),
\]
and define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:global-pair-rank-definition}
W_{\mathrm{pair}}(M)=
\bigoplus_{\{p,q\}\subseteq E(M)}W_{p,q}(M),\qquad
\mathfrak q(M)=\dim_kW_{\mathrm{pair}}(M).
\end{equation}
Loops contribute zero to these spaces; in statements about actual vertices
they are simply omitted. The value of $\mathfrak q(M)$ is independent of $k$. Define also the
standard-degree-zero one-link rank
\begin{equation}\label{eq:degree-zero-pair-rank-definition}
\mathfrak q_0(M)=
\sum_{e\in V(M)}
\sum_{\{p,q\}\subseteq V(\operatorname{lk}_M e)}
\dim_kT^2_{2\mathbf e_e-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(M),
\end{equation}
where loops in the link are omitted.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- theorem-19: body_md -->
\label{thm:global-pair-rank}
The direct sum of the pure-pair cup products is a split epimorphism
\[
\mu_M:
\bigoplus_{\{p,q\}\subseteq E(M)}V_p(M)\otimes_kV_q(M)
\twoheadrightarrow W_{\mathrm{pair}}(M)
\]
over every field, and it has an integral split form.  Moreover,
\begin{align}
\mathfrak q(M)
&=\sum_{\{p,q\}\subseteq E(M)}
\sum_{\substack{H\text{ hyperplane of }M^*\\
H\cap\{p,q\}=\varnothing}}
\bigl(|\mathcal G_{\{p,q\}}(H)|-1\bigr)_+,
\label{eq:global-pair-rank-formula}\\
\mathfrak q(M)=0
&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
M\text{ has no }U_{1,4}\text{-minor}.
\label{eq:global-pair-rank-vanishing}
\end{align}
If $D$ is a cocircuit of cardinality $d\ge4$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:global-pair-cocircuit-bound}
\mathfrak q(M)\ge\binom d2(d-3).
\end{equation}
If $M$ is connected with rank at least two and corank at least three, then
the direct sum of the link-lifted cup products is split surjective onto the
space counted by $\mathfrak q_0(M)$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:degree-zero-pair-cocircuit-bound}
\mathfrak q_0(M)\ge\binom d2(d-3)
\end{equation}
for some cocircuit $D$ of cardinality $d\ge4$ in a one-element contraction
of $M$.
<!-- end theorem-19 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
Theorem~\ref{thm:integral-pair} gives a split epimorphism for each unordered
pair; taking direct sums proves the first assertion.  The pair formula
\eqref{eq:pair-dim} gives \eqref{eq:global-pair-rank-formula}, and the
vanishing equivalence follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:vanishing}, since the
pair layer detects the full $T^2$-vanishing locus.

For each pair in a cocircuit $D$, Proposition~\ref{prop:pure-cocircuit}
gives a target of dimension at least $d-3$.  The corresponding fine degrees
are distinct, so summing over the $\binom d2$ pairs proves
\eqref{eq:global-pair-cocircuit-bound}.  For the standard-degree-zero
assertion, choose $e$ and a connected component of $M/e$ as in
Lemma~\ref{lem:one-contraction}.  Apply the same cocircuit argument in that
link and transport the integral right inverses by
Corollary~\ref{cor:link-lifted-cup}.  This proves split surjectivity and
\eqref{eq:degree-zero-pair-cocircuit-bound}.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- corollary-19: body_md -->
\label{cor:pair-rank-direct-sum}
For matroids on disjoint ground sets,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pair-rank-direct-sum}
\mathfrak q(M_1\oplus M_2)=\mathfrak q(M_1)+\mathfrak q(M_2).
\end{equation}
More precisely, a pair with one element in each summand has zero target,
whereas a pair contained in one summand has the same target as in that
summand.
<!-- end corollary-19 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Take the degree $-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q$ part of \eqref{eq:direct-sum-T2}.  If $p$ and
$q$ lie in different summands, each potential tensor term would require a
negative degree in a Stanley--Reisner ring factor, which is impossible.  If
both lie in one summand, the degree-zero part of the other ring is $k$ and
the target is unchanged.  Summing over unordered pairs proves
\eqref{eq:pair-rank-direct-sum}.
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- corollary-20: body_md -->
\label{cor:rank-two-pure-pair-rank}
Let $M$ be a loopless rank-two matroid with parallel classes
$P_1,\ldots,P_t$ of sizes $n_1,\ldots,n_t$, and put $n=\sum_i n_i$.  Then
\begin{align}
\mathfrak q(M)={}&
\sum_i\binom{n_i}{2}
\left(n_i-3+
\sum_{\substack{a<c\\a,c\ne i}}n_an_c\right)_+
\label{eq:rank-two-pair-rank}\\
&+\sum_{i<j}n_in_j
\sum_{k\ne i,j}n_k(n-3-n_k)_+.
\nonumber
\end{align}
For the rank-one uniform matroid,
\[
\mathfrak q(U_{1,n})=\binom n2(n-3)_+.
\]
<!-- end corollary-20 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Sum the within-class case of Theorem~\ref{thm:rank-two-formulas} over the
$\binom{n_i}{2}$ pairs in $P_i$, and sum the between-class case over the
$n_in_j$ pairs in $P_i\times P_j$.  The rank-one formula follows directly
from the single cocircuit of $U_{1,n}$.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- theorem-20: body_md -->
\label{thm:rank-two-pair-extremum}
Among connected loopless rank-two matroids of corank $c\ge3$, the sharp
minimum of the global pure-pair obstruction rank is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-two-pair-minimum}
\min\mathfrak q(M)=
\begin{cases}
6,&c=3,\\
26,&c=4,\\
\dfrac{c(c-2)(c+3)}2,&c\ge5.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
Writing the parallel-class sizes as an unordered partition of $c+2$, the
equality profiles are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-two-pair-equality}
(2,2,1),\qquad(3,2,1),\qquad(c,1,1)\quad(c\ge5),
\end{equation}
respectively.  Thus the equality profile is unique up to permutation for
every $c\ge3$.
<!-- end theorem-20 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
For a class profile $\nu=(n_1,\ldots,n_t)$, write $Q(\nu)$ for the
right-hand side of \eqref{eq:rank-two-pair-rank}.  Put $n=c+2$ and
$C=n-3$.  For each index $i$, let
\[
e_i=\sum_{\substack{j<\ell\\j,\ell\ne i}}n_jn_\ell.
\]
Regrouping the second sum by the omitted class gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pair-rank-regrouped}
Q(\nu)=\sum_i\binom{n_i}{2}(n_i-3+e_i)
+\sum_i n_i(C-n_i)_+e_i.
\end{equation}
The first positive part from \eqref{eq:rank-two-pair-rank} is unnecessary:
for a profile with at least three classes and $n\ge5$, one has
$n_i-3+e_i\ge0$.

Suppose $t\ge4$ and merge classes of sizes $x,y$ into a class of size
$z=x+y$.  Let $R$ be the remaining list, and put
\[
S=\sum_{r\in R}r,\qquad E=\sum_{r<s\in R}rs.
\]
Every original class has size at most $C$, while $z\le C+1$.  If $z\le C$,
direct subtraction in \eqref{eq:pair-rank-regrouped} gives
\begin{align}
2\bigl(Q(\nu)-Q(\nu')\bigr)
=xy\Biggl(&2\sum_{r\in R}\left[\binom r2+r(C-r)\right]
+8-3z\nonumber\\
&+S(4C-z-2)+2E\Biggr)>0.
\label{eq:pair-rank-merge}
\end{align}
Indeed, $S\ge2$, and the expression not already visibly nonnegative is at
least $4+8C-5z\ge4+3C$.  If $z=C+1$, necessarily $R=(1,1)$, and subtraction
reduces to
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pair-rank-merge-boundary}
2\bigl(Q(\nu)-Q(\nu')\bigr)=xy(7C-3)-2C-2>0,
\end{equation}
because $xy\ge C$ and $C\ge2$.  Repeated merging strictly decreases $Q$,
so a minimizer has exactly three classes.

Let $a\le b\le d$ and $a+b+d=n$.  Except for $(a,b,d)=(1,1,c)$, all three
terms $C-a,C-b,C-d$ are nonnegative, and
\begin{align}
2Q(a,b,d)={}&a(a-1)(a-3+bd)+b(b-1)(b-3+ad)\nonumber\\
&+d(d-1)(d-3+ab)+2abd(2n-9).
\label{eq:pair-rank-three-classes}
\end{align}
If $a\ge2$, set $A=a-1$, $U=b-a$, and $V=d-b$.  Subtracting the value after
the transfer $(a,b,d)\mapsto(a-1,b,d+1)$ gives
\begin{align}
2\bigl(Q(a,b,d)-Q(a-1,b,d+1)\bigr)
={}&15A^2+3A-4+(15A^2+28A-3)U\nonumber\\
&+(15A^2+8A-2)V+11U^2+2V^2+8UV\nonumber\\
&+25AU^2+30AUV+5AV^2\nonumber\\
&+10U^3+15U^2V+5UV^2>0.
\label{eq:pair-rank-transfer}
\end{align}
All coefficients in the first line are positive for $A\ge1$, and the other
terms are nonnegative.  Iteration reduces every minimizer to $(1,b,d)$.

Put $s=b+d=c+1$ and $p=bd$.  For $b\ge2$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pair-rank-one-b-d}
2Q(1,b,d)=s(s-1)(s-3)+2(s-4)p.
\end{equation}
The product $p=b(s-b)$ is minimized on $2\le b\le s/2$ at $b=2$.  The
exceptional profile has value
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pair-rank-concentrated}
Q(1,1,c)=\frac{c(c-2)(c+3)}2.
\end{equation}
For $b=2$, the difference between \eqref{eq:pair-rank-one-b-d} and
\eqref{eq:pair-rank-concentrated} is $c^2-6c+6$.  This is negative for
$c=3,4$ and positive for every $c\ge5$.  The cases $c=3,4$ give the first
two profiles in \eqref{eq:rank-two-pair-equality}, while the concentrated
profile is uniquely minimizing for $c\ge5$.  Strictness in the merge,
transfer, and product comparisons proves uniqueness.
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- corollary-21: body_md -->
\label{cor:rank-two-pair-stability}
Let $c\ge5$.  If a connected loopless rank-two matroid of corank $c$ does
not have class profile $(c,1,1)$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-two-pair-stability}
\mathfrak q(M)\ge
\frac{c(c-2)(c+3)}2+c^2-6c+6.
\end{equation}
Equality holds exactly for the profile $(c-1,2,1)$, up to permutation.
<!-- end corollary-21 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
Among nonextremal three-class profiles, the transfer calculation reduces to
$(1,b,c+1-b)$ with $b\ge2$.  Equation~\eqref{eq:pair-rank-one-b-d} and the
monotonicity of $b(c+1-b)$ show that the unique minimum occurs at $b=2$,
and its difference from \eqref{eq:pair-rank-concentrated} is
$c^2-6c+6$.  If a profile has at least four classes, merging strictly lowers
$Q$.  When the final three-class profile is nonextremal, the preceding bound
is strict.  If the final profile is $(1,1,c)$, the penultimate profile is
$(1,1,x,y)$ with $x+y=c$, and
\eqref{eq:pair-rank-merge-boundary} gives
\[
2\bigl(Q(1,1,x,y)-Q(1,1,c)\bigr)
=xy(7c-10)-2c,
\]
which is strictly larger than $2(c^2-6c+6)$ for $c\ge5$.  Equality can
therefore occur only for $(1,2,c-1)$.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
The invariants $\mathfrak q(M)$ and $\Theta(M)=\dim_kT^2(M)_0$ are different
in rank two.  The sharp values in \eqref{eq:rank-two-pair-minimum} measure
the complete purely negative pair layer, whereas
Theorem~\ref{thm:rank-two-extremum} measures the standard-degree-zero
one-link layer.  Thus the pair layer begins with $6,26,\ldots$, while the
degree-zero layer begins with $6,32,81,168,\ldots$.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- theorem-21: body_md -->
\label{thm:degree-zero-master}
For every finite matroid $M$ and every field $k$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:degree-zero-master}
\dim_kT^2(M)_0=
\sum_{\substack{\varnothing\ne A\in M}}
\sum_{\substack{B\subseteq V(L_A)\\|B|\ge2}}
\binom{|B|-1}{|A|-1}\,\omega_M(A,B).
\end{equation}
In particular, the standard-degree-zero obstruction dimension is
characteristic-independent and is computable from finitely many flat graphs
in the links of independent sets.
<!-- end theorem-21 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
Fix a positive support $A$ of size $s$ and a negative support $B$ of size
$b$.  The link localization formula identifies the corresponding fine
component with $T^2_{-\mathbf 1_B}(L_A)$, and hence its dimension is
$\omega_M(A,B)$.  The standard total degree is zero exactly when the sum of
the positive exponents is $b$.  The number of positive exponent vectors with
support exactly $A$ and total sum $b$ is
\[
\#\{(u_a)_{a\in A}:u_a\ge1,\ \sum_{a\in A}u_a=b\}
=\binom{b-1}{s-1},
\]
with the usual convention that this is zero for $b<s$.  The empty positive
support cannot contribute because $B$ is nonempty.  Summing over $A$ and
$B$ proves \eqref{eq:degree-zero-master}; the graph formula gives the
characteristic independence.
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- corollary-22: body_md -->
\label{cor:degree-zero-algorithm}
For a rank-$r$ matroid, equation \eqref{eq:degree-zero-master} only requires
independent supports $A$ with $1\le|A|\le r-1$.  A fixed graph block with
negative support $B$ is counted with the binomial multiplicity
$\binom{|B|-1}{|A|-1}$.  Thus the standard-degree-zero slice is a finite
rank-stratified incidence invariant, rather than a separate cohomology
calculation.
<!-- end corollary-22 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
If $|A|\ge r$, its link has rank zero and has no actual vertex supporting a
nonzero negative component.  The remaining assertion is the coefficient
count in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:degree-zero-master}.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- theorem-22: body_md -->
\label{thm:rank-three-formula}
For every simple rank-three matroid $M$ on $n$ elements and every field $k$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rank-three-formula}
\dim_kT^2(M)_0=\Theta_3(M)+\sum_{e\in E(M)}\Phi_e(M).
\end{equation}
Consequently the entire standard-degree-zero dimension is determined by the
global line sizes and the line-pencil partitions at the points.
<!-- end theorem-22 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
The support criterion allows positive support of size at most two.  If
$|A|=2$, simplicity makes $A$ independent and its link has rank one.  Degree
zero forces a negative pair, and the rank-one-link formula contributes
$f(n-|\operatorname{cl}_M(A)|)$.  Grouping pairs $A$ with the same line closure gives
$\Theta_3(M)$.

If $A=\{e\}$, the link $M/e$ is rank two and its parallel classes are
$L_i(e)\setminus\{e\}$ of sizes $m_{e,i}$.  The rank-two formula has three
possible negative supports.  A pair in one class gives the first line of
\eqref{eq:rank-three-point-formula}; a pair in two different classes gives
the second line; and a triple from three classes survives exactly when,
after removing the selected points, at most one parallel class remains,
which is the condition $\rho_e(I)\le1$.  The coefficient in the latter case
is $(n-5)_+$.  Summing over $e$ proves the formula.  No other positive
support contributes, and all terms are graph dimensions, so the result is
characteristic-independent.
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- corollary-23: body_md -->
\label{cor:uniform-rank-three}
For $n\ge6$,
\[
\dim_kT^2(U_{3,n})_0=
\binom n2\binom{n-2}{2}(n-5)
+n\binom{n-1}{2}(n-3)(n-5).
\]
<!-- end corollary-23 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
Every line has two points, and every point pencil has $n-1$ singleton
classes.  Substitute these data into \eqref{eq:rank-three-formula}; the
triple term is zero.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- corollary-24: body_md -->
\label{cor:fano-rank-three}
For the Fano matroid $F_7$,
\[
\dim_kT^2(F_7)_0=357
\]
over every field.
<!-- end corollary-24 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
The seven lines each have three points. Contracting any point gives three
parallel classes of size two, not singleton classes. Thus
\[
\Theta_3(F_7)=7\binom32\binom42(4-3)=126.
\]
For the partition $(2,2,2)$, the first two lines of
\eqref{eq:rank-three-point-formula} contribute $9$ and $24$, respectively;
the last line vanishes because $\rho_e(\{1,2,3\})=3$. Hence
$\Phi_e(F_7)=33$ and the total is $126+7\cdot33=357$.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- theorem-23: body_md -->
\label{thm:cocircuit-reconstruction-new}
Let $M$ be loopless of rank $r\ge2$ and suppose every cocircuit has size at
least four.  Then the labeled profile $\mathscr W_M$ determines $M$ up to
relabeling.  More precisely, for every independent $(r-1)$-set $A$, if
\[
D_A=\{p:\mathscr W_M(A;p,q)>0\text{ for some }q\},
\]
then $D_A=E(M)\setminus\operatorname{cl}_M(A)$, and these sets recover all cocircuits.
<!-- end theorem-23 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
The rank-one-link formula gives
\[
\mathscr W_M(A;p,q)=
\begin{cases}
|D_A|-3,&A\in M,\ p,q\in D_A,\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
The cocircuit hypothesis makes the first case nonzero for every independent
$A$, so the union of the negative-coordinate supports is exactly $D_A$.
Every hyperplane has a basis of size $r-1$, and cocircuits determine the
matroid.  Hence the profile reconstructs $M$.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- theorem-24: body_md -->
\label{thm:rank-three-rigidity-new}
Let $M$ and $M'$ be simple rank-three matroids on the same labeled ground set
$E$, with $|E|=n\ge7$.  If
\[
\dim_kT^2_{\mathbf e_a+\mathbf e_b-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(M)
=\dim_kT^2_{\mathbf e_a+\mathbf e_b-\mathbf e_p-\mathbf e_q}(M')
\]
for all disjoint unordered pairs $\{a,b\}$ and $\{p,q\}$, then
$M=M'$.  In fact, only the nonvanishing pattern is needed.
<!-- end theorem-24 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
Fix $A=\{a,b\}$.  Its closure is a line $L_A$, and the rank-one-link
formula says that the profile is nonzero precisely when
$|E\setminus L_A|\ge4$; in that case the union of the negative supports is
$E\setminus L_A$.  Thus every detected line is recovered.

Define the zero-profile graph on $E$ by joining $a,b$ when all the
components with positive support $\{a,b\}$ in the statement vanish.
Its edges are exactly the pairs contained in undetected lines.
An undetected line has size at least $n-3$. For $n\ge8$ two distinct such
lines cannot coexist, since distinct lines meet in at most one point.  For
$n=7$ there are at most two; if there are two, they are four-point lines
meeting in one point and are the maximal cliques of the zero-profile graph.
In either case its maximal cliques of size at least two are exactly the
undetected lines; isolated vertices do not represent lines.
Hence the undetected lines are also recovered. The rank-two flats determine
a simple rank-three matroid, proving the assertion.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
<!-- corollary-25: body_md -->
\label{cor:rank-three-inverse-algorithm}
For a simple rank-three matroid on $n\ge7$ labeled elements, the lines can be
reconstructed in polynomial time from the nonzero components with positive
support a pair and negative support a pair: take the complement of the union
of the negative supports for every detected pair, and recover any remaining
large lines as maximal cliques in the zero-profile graph.
<!-- end corollary-25 -->
<!-- proof-51: body_md -->
This is the constructive procedure in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:rank-three-rigidity-new}. The nonisolated part of the
zero-profile graph is a union of at most two cliques meeting in at most
one vertex. For each edge, its endpoints together with their common
neighbors recover its clique; removing duplicates therefore finds all
the required cliques in polynomial time. Testing a candidate triple
against the recovered line list decides independence.
<!-- end proof-51 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:rigidity-sharpness}
The bound $n\ge7$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:rank-three-rigidity-new} is sharp.  On
six labeled points, a pair is detected exactly when its line has two points,
and the detected block then carries the data
$(d_A-3,E\setminus A)=(1,E\setminus A)$, which depends only on the pair
itself.  The two copies of $M(K_4)$ with line sets
\[
\{123,\,145,\,246,\,356\}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\{124,\,135,\,236,\,456\}
\]
both have exactly the two-point lines $16$, $25$, and $34$, so their labeled
profiles coincide, while the matroids differ.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:pencil-concentration-new}
Let $L$ be a line of a simple rank-three matroid on $n=l+d$ elements, with
$l\ge4$ and $d\ge4$, and suppose $L$ is a longest line.  If $e\notin L$,
then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pencil-concentration}
\Phi_e(M)\ge
\tau(l,d):=\binom{l-1}{2}d(3l+2d-14)
+3\binom{l-1}{3}(l+d-5).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-52: body_md -->
The classes of the pencil at $e$ have sizes $m_1,\ldots,m_t$, where
$t\ge l$, $\sum_i m_i=n-1$, and $m_i\le d$. Retain the second line of
\eqref{eq:rank-three-point-formula}, which counts pairs from different
classes. Since $m_i\le d=n-l\le n-4$, its positive parts can be removed.
Grouping its three contributions for each unordered triple of indices gives
\[
F_n(m_1,\ldots,m_t)=
\sum_{i<j<k}m_im_jm_k
\bigl(3(n-4)-m_i-m_j-m_k\bigr).
\]
For a list of remaining entries $R$ with sum $S$ and second elementary
symmetric function $E_2(R)$, splitting an entry $a+b$ changes this
quantity by
\[
ab\bigl(S(2n-11)+4E_2(R)\bigr)\ge0.
\]
Thus merging two entries whose sum is at most $d$ cannot increase $F_n$.
If there are more than $l$ entries, two entries have sum at most $d$;
otherwise, for the two smallest entries $a\le b$,
\[
\sum_i m_i\ge a+lb\ge\frac{(l+1)(d+1)}2>l+d-1,
\]
which is impossible.  Merge until there are $l$ entries.  With two entries
$2\le a\le b<d$ fixed, transferring one unit from $a$ to $b$ changes $F_n$ by
\[
-(b-a+1)\bigl(S(2n-11)+4E_2(R)\bigr)\le0.
\]
Iteration gives the extremal list $(d,1,\ldots,1)$, and substitution gives
\eqref{eq:pencil-concentration}.  The other summands in
\eqref{eq:rank-three-point-formula} are nonnegative.
<!-- end proof-52 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
